projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Frank Girman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Frank Girman. Mr. Girman served in the U.S. Army Aircorps with the 8th Air Force, 384th Bomb Group, 546th Squadron. He served in the European theater, and his highest rank was Tech Sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Girman's home in Brunswick, Ohio, on March 30th, 2004. Frank was 81 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Mile from here, in Weymouth. My dad lived there, what, since 1929, we moved out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When were you born?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: March 12th, I just turned 81. March --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What, oh, just turned 81.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: March 12th, 1923.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you -- let's see. Were you still in school in 1941, then?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No. I graduated in '40.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I think I was at work. I worked at Ohio Crankshaft at the time. I believe I was at work then, because we worked a lot of overtime. Sundays was nothing, nothing unusual, to be working.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you heard the news about the attack, what was your reaction?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Hmm. I was surprised. That was obvious, for everybody. But I don't think I had any particular reaction to it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did many of the people you worked with, did any of them decide to go out and sign up?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, a few of them did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, well, I tried to enlist, too; but they turned me down, because I, color, 'scuse me, partially color blind. Then they went and drafted me in the Air Force anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you tried to enlist in the Army Air Corps?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then when were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: 1943? Yeah, I went in in 1943. January.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything for the war effort in that year or so before you went in, anything back on the home front?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, of course working for Ohio Crankshaft, we were making crankshafts for all kinds of engines. But other than that, not, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't get involved in scrap drives or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was rationing much of a problem that first year?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No. Not for me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why not for you?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I didn't do the shopping. The only thing we had with rationing one time was, I was home on leave, and I blew two tires within a mile of one another. But that was about the -- trying to get tires was not a easy chore at that time. But other than that, being in the service, rationing was no problem to me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you went into the Army in early '43; right?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, January '43.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you first went into the Army, was it a tough adjustment to be there with guys from all over the country?Frank Girman:: No, not at all. Every -- well, started out with, of course, I was, went to Camp Perry. I was, went with some friends, you know. But after that, no. I went to St. Petersburg, I knew nobody. But there was no problem. Everybody was in the same boat. So -- we knew we had to get along. We did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about basic training?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, I went to St. Petersburg. The first week was very nice, living in a hotel; and after that, we went out to the swamps, tent city. And they closed it down, just shortly after I left, because there's spinal meningitis outbreak. Closed it down. Well, a friend of mine, Carl Roub, he had spinal meningitis, he was down there with me. And well, they closed down, I left, went to Lincoln, Nebraska.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, do you remember any stories from basic training, anything out of the ordinary?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, just one little item. There's a baby rattler on top of my buddy's bed one night. But there was a lot of rattle snakes. We were the first ones into the tent city, you know; and there was a lot of snakes around.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what did you do with the baby rattler?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: It wasn't me. It was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was your buddy?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, the guy next to me. He just took the cover and flipped 'em, the -- there was nothing else to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No snakes were harmed.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what were you trained as?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I trained airplane mechanic.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As a mechanic. Ground crew?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, I never was ground crew.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: But, and then we went to Lincoln, Nebraska. From Lincoln, I went to a factory, what they called factory school at the time, Las Vegas; and Burbank, California, and spent the time there. And there, went to gunnery school. And gunnery school, came home. Late getting back. Trained, blew the side arm on the drive wheels, those, were sitting there for, I don't know, a day I think before they got, sent another engine out to get us out of there. But school was uneventful.Thomas Swope:: Gunnery school, nothing unusual happened. Anything you can tell me about that?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: In school?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Gunnery school in Las Vegas?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No. Other than some, the guns were a little hot and got cooked off, and took everybody by surprise when they started rattling. But that was about all. The only thing that struck my mind was, in gunnery school, was, we had to shoot at a trap from a turret on the back of a pickup gun (sic). And it's not easy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: In fact, I think I missed. But that, gunnery school was nothing spectacular. Las Vegas, that was fun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you spend time in Las Vegas?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah. That's where the gunnery school was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not a whole lot in Las Vegas at that time, was there?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, Frontier Street. But there was enough to keep us busy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now how fast was that pickup truck moving when you were trying to shoot?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I don't really know. Probably about 15, 20 miles an hour.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: It's only strictly a guess. I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And would you try to shoot at a stationary target, or --

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, clay pigeons.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, they were shooting clay pigeons --

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- on you. So they were going one direction, you were going --

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: They were going the other one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was anybody able to hit anything like that?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I don't think there was too many. Not, not in our group, anyway. But basically I enjoyed my time in the Army. I didn't have no really bad memories. Just, you know, personal bad memories.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What came next after gunnery school?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, long story. Somehow I got mixed up in orders. We got to Rapid City, South Dakota. Now, what is it, Ellsworth? I think it's now Ellsworth Air Base. And just start a crew, but they just started a crew. There was nothing for about 90 of us to do but loaf for the first three months. And of course, as usual, we're young, we were all over the country, 'cause we had nothing to do. The Army paid (inaudible) very well. All got back but one. He was the guy that lived closest to the base. But that, about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Then what happened next? Were you assigned to a crew then?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yes. We were known as -- of course, our pilot was Ted Muller. Very good pilot. Excellent pilot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Good pilot?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with all the crew?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of planes were you flying?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: There she is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh yeah. Did you like the B-17?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Hey,it got me back, yeah. No problem there. 17 was a very good airplane. Took a beating, came back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your position?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I was the engineer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Engineer. And would that make you top gunner then?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Top gunner, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you go overseas then?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, I went overseas. Went to, with the 384th bomb group, flew my 35 missions.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you go overseas?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: It was right around D-Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right around D-Day?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I can't tell you the exact. My son's got all my records. I gave them to him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you fly or ship overseas?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Flew.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did fly.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah. One little incident there, on -- we took off from Grenier Field, bound for Goose Bay, Labrador, which we arrived; but I mean, the desolation of the place, you wouldn't believe. But from there, we were going to Iceland. And we were out over the water maybe half an hour or so, and one of the engines started to run away. So the pilot asked me what to do. I'm supposed to be the technical expert on the airplane. And I told him to run the props through, which is meaning, going from full pitch to low pitch. And somehow he didn't think I was right, so he turned around and went back. When he turned around, went back, we were met by a reception committee. And he asked the pilot, he says, "You ask your engineer what to do?" He said yes. He said, "He tell you?" He told him. He says, "Get in the blankity-blank airplane, and next time, listen to him." Right. We got to Iceland, we were fogbound over there for a week or two. And then went to, we landed in Wales, I can never remember the name of the place. And then what they called Wash in England, big indentation for gunnery school, or the tactics that, you know, they used at the time. And we got assigned to the 384 from there.Flew my missions.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first mission?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Where we went, I don't know. But yeah, we were up all night. We're a little apprehensive, to say the least.Thomas Swope:: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: It turned out to be a rather uneventful mission. Nothing particularly harmful.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it a mission over Germany, do you think, or France?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, I think it was Germany, but I couldn't tell you. I got the list. But I can't tell you right now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, specifics doesn't really matter. Now would that have been shortly after D-Day, then, when you flew that first mission?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So as far as that first mission, mostly you remember being a little bit afraid?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah. Well, we should be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: But we didn't see any, as I recall, we didn't have -- a little bit of flak; but no, didn't see no planes. As a matter of fact, we didn't see many planes for the whole mission, for the whole time we were there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Whole tour?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: If I had to guess right now, I'd say probably two, maybe three. That would be about all we ever saw of German planes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you said you did fly 35 missions?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you completed your tour of duty?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the tour right then, 35?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: It was 30 when I first got there, but they stretched it to 35.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So any other memorable missions you can tell me about?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, when I got the plexiglass blown off the top of my head.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Let's hear about it.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, I don't, again, I don't know where we were flying. But a piece of flak hit it, and it broke the plexiglass behind my head. Of course in the upper turret, only your head is out of the airplane. And I guess I got a little bit loud on the inter -- the mike, 'cause I was screaming that I was hit. The copilot turned, got out of the seat, turned around and looked at me, and started laughing. I didn't have a scratch on me; just the plexiglass going down my neck. I had all kinds of visions of blood streaming down my neck. But I never got a scratch. And, well, not, didn't happen to me, but our C.O. kind of, we used to tie our shoes on the back of our parachute, or parachute harness, in case you had to jump; because you couldn't walk in the flight booth very well. And he got them shot off of his back end, just as neat as if you took a pair of scissors. Nothing -- he didn't get hit. No, nobody got a scratch on them in our whole crew, except our copilot; he died. But not with us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: With, flying in a different plane, he died?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah. Well, we became lead crew, what they call, we flew the radar, excuse me, the radar plane. Or, and the pathfinder, what they call them then. And we don't know the particulars. We know that he was making an emergency landing, and he crashed. But we don't know the particulars of the flight or not. But he was the only casualty that I know of. Whatever happened after that, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what else can you tell me? What can you tell me about flying the pathfinder?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, you were lead crew, so-called lead crew. And everybody dropped on you. And it took longer to complete the tour, because you didn't fly as often as you normally would. And if you're -- usually the copilot seat was a colonel or somebody pretty well up there. He was, led the formation, you know. In charge of the formation, I should say. But of course we lost our ball turret gunner when that happened. And -- because the radar, the dome took the place of the ball turret. And we picked up another officer, flew in the radio room; but that was about it. One story that, we went to -- my parents came from Czechoslovakia. And I flew a mission with, to Brux, Czechoslovakia. I can't find it on the map. I know where it's supposed to be, but I can't find it on any map. But it was just north of, northwest of Prague. And when we came back, I wrote a letter to -- couldn't figure out how to tell my parents that I'd flown to Czechoslovakia; so I said, "I went to visit my grandparents." All hell broke loose. I had the Red Cross after me. Was I shot down? Where was I? My mother was all up in arms. But I, I'll never forget that, her reactions to the letter. I was just trying to tell her the simple thing that I flew over Czechoslovakia, and never expecting the results I got.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would that town have been anywhere near Kemnitz, Czechoslovakia?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, it's not too far from the German border. If I recall correctly, we flew north of Berlin, then we made, went down into Czechoslovakia. And that was one of the occasions that we got hit by fighters. But I wasn't hit. We weren't. Though one flew right over us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I know I got, oh, I don't know how -- I was angry. I couldn't depress the guns enough to shoot at 'em. But I got a shot at him going away, but I doubt that I hit him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that about as close as you got to hitting one?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: That was as close as I got to hitting one. Yeah, he flew right between us and our, he flew, the triangle formation, you know, and he flew right to the right of us, right over our wings. And you, I could see him, it was an ME-109. I could see the pilot. We were very -- well, you don't get much closer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How close do you think that was; can you judge at all?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, our wing span was 103 feet, so that was on the right side, our wing was what, 50 feet. And he probably was in 60, 70 feet of us. And he was between us and the plane flying off of our right wing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Pretty darn close. And I never thought of it until now, I don't remember him firing at us. And if he wasn't, 'cause I did -- where he was, I mean, well of course he could have hit our wing tip, but he wouldn't have hit the plane from where he was. And he was so close he couldn't turn into us, because then we would have had a midair collision. But I often told Ray, Ray Schultz, I mean, 'cause he's kind of, thinks I'm somebody, because I flew missions, but it -- what happened to you was, fighter planes was where you were in the formation. They could have a group ahead of you getting the heck shot out of them, and you probably never saw a plane, or if you were in the back end, depending where -- so your position in the bomber stream was a great deal to do with how much action you saw. And fortunately for us, I didn't see too much. Don't, I have to tell a story on myself. And if memory serves me, it was the mission that flew to Brux, because it as a long way for us, maximum endurance, or pretty close. And so we had, the Tokyo tanks were full of gas. You only use them when you were going long distance or maximum amount, bomb load. And each tank, after the main tanks, each tank got progressively smaller, 'cause they were filling the ribs, all the way out to the end of the wing. If memory serves me, the last tank held about five gallons. And they drain by gravity, into the main tanks. But you didn't use them for take-off. You used the main tanks for take-off. But after we were in formation, switched over to them, opened up the valve, so that they, the gasoline drained into the main tanks. And you had no way of knowing -- it was a timing thing. Supposed to have them open for about 45 minutes to an hour. And you closed them up, because you didn't want gas vapors circulating. And looked at my watch and, well later, oh, hour's up. Shut them off. It was about 10 minutes had gone by. And coming back, why, we, gas tanks are a little bit low. We had some doubts whether we were going to make it. I said well, what the heck. Maybe there's a little bit of gas left. I opened up the valves. The gas gauge never moved from that, they just sat on empty for the last 45 minutes of the flight. The gas was flowing in just fast enough for the, keeping up with the engine consumption. I never told the pilot that, either. I don't know why, but I never did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He thought you were a miracle worker or something.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: But those things happen. I misread the clock, the time, and damn near paid the price, not only me but everybody. And swimming in the channel is kind of cold. We didn't particularly like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there any targets that you really dreaded going after?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah. Schweinfurt. And oil targets were heavily defended. It wasn't -- not for us. I mean, it was riding the flak coming through, going through. You could see it in front of you, and you knew you were going to go into it, and you knew you didn't want to go into it. But I don't know, for me the strangest thing, I didn't, by no matter I mean did I like it; but the most terrifying to me, and for some reason, I have no reason why I can't tell you, was after we dropped the bombs, you flew straight for awhile, so, clear everything behind you, then you turned to go back home. And I hated looking down the wing at the ground. 'Cause you could see, sometimes you could see the flashes, you know, the artillery. And I, I would, I was deadly afraid of looking town for some reason. But I mean, height didn't bother me, flying didn't bother me at all. Just looking down at the ground, knowing that that's where all those flak bursts were coming from. And I just, I don't know whether it was, I, afraid of it mentally or whatever it was, I don't know. But I mean, I just -- but yet I couldn't stop looking. I still had to look down, every time we turned. But no, there ain't a hell of a lot more, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So any other memorable missions that you made?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, we flew to Cologne a lot. In fact, most of my missions, believe it or not, were in the Ruhr Valley, which was probably the most heavily defended area. It was the industrial area, excuse me, industrial area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: And I know for the, went to Cologne, we used to bomb the railroad junction right alongside the old Cologne cathedral. And we used the cathedral for the aiming point. That's what we released our bombs on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But always missed the cathedral?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Not always. But it survived the war. It did get hit a few times, but nothing serious. There was no direct hits on it, that I know of. And I always glad, thought it strange, you're bombing some famous structure, and I'm a little bit of a history buff anyway. And I didn't want to see the cathedral blown, but yet I knew that's what our aiming point was. 'Cause right alongside of it was the railroad marshalling yards. That's one of the things we always flew at. As a matter of fact, we flew round-robin, we flew -- when we weren't in troops, we flew the oil targets, transportation targets, and then the manufacturing. When we got done with them, we just started all over again. And of course they obvious, as soon as knock the oil out, which we succeeded in doing very well, we cut their production practically down to nothing. And they couldn't move their tanks. No grease, no oil, no -- they couldn't fly the airplanes, either. That was one reason why we saw so little opposition.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How much time off did you get between missions?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: It depended. We probably -- weather had a big factor, was always a big factor. We took off on ice one time. Wasn't ice, but I mean, it was, kind of slushy stuff. And had a little trouble getting off. I mean off the ground, but we made it. And the funny part, I don't remember the name of the castle, but it was maybe about five miles off the end of our runway, the one with all the windows in it. And we flew kind of low over it, not because we wanted to, because of the weather.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Probably rattled a few windows. I remember one time the airplane ran off, of all the places, right where the runways intersected, and they had to scrub a mission, and that didn't sit very well.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do on your time off in England?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, not a hell of a lot; because you couldn't go nowhere, really. We were, Grafton Underwood was our code name, also the town where we were situated. And that was just a little burg, maybe couple hundred residents. And from there, you had to go to Northampton. And that was probably 25, 30 miles away. We didn't have no transportation, you know. Well, they did have liberty runs; but you had to go over there, but what do you do? You drink, you watch the people go by; and England during the war time was kind of, nothing happening, you know, as far as the towns. Of course London was always hustle and bustle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You have much contact with the British people?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Quite a bit, on leave, yeah. Had quite a bit of contact with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nice?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: The me they were very nice. A couple of them, I know they couldn't afford it. I was making more money than they were. But they, they bought us dinner, you know, occasionally. And I had no bad experiences with them at all. The only thing is, I couldn't understand, says you can't miss it, but I never found what I was looking for. Strange, I mean, they have a lot of circles. They call them circles, traffic circles.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: And I get lost on those all the time; 'cause you go over there, what street did they come down from, you turn around, and they all look identical. If you didn't look up at the sign, you don't know which where you came from. I was lost always in London. But we got around. Westminister Abbey, went to Buckingham Palace, and wherever. Most of our activity was centered around Picadilly Circus. 'Cause that's where the Red Cross was. And well, Trafalgar Square. The subways of course. I slept in them a few nights, 'cause you couldn't get a hotel room for nothing. Practically impossible.Just went down to the air raid shelters and slept. At least that's what we did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Have much of a problem with buzz bombs at that time?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I never saw a buzz bomb. I was over there. But I did get woke up by a V-2.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: It was nowheres near us. I mean, the concussion and stuff, the shock waves. It woke me up from a nice beautiful, dead sleep. The damage in east London was, I can't describe it. I mean, it's -- there weren't no buildings standing. Very few buildings, you know, or, that weren't somehow damaged. But people lived. They lived in them. I don't -- it wasn't an easy life; that's for sure. They manage. But of course, I was only in London, what, three or four times. One other incident, a friend of mine, Ralph Simons, he is passed away now, he lived just about a mile and a half from here, he was in the 381st bomb group. And I went to visit him. And he was a crew chief. And stood in his little shack alongside the hard stand, and decided we were going to go get a cup of coffee. When we came back, there was no shanty left. Plane coming back from a mission, well, they crashed and wiped it out. Otherwise he and I both would have been sitting in it. But well, that's the thing. I mean, it's a game of inches I guess, you know. That's with a they call football. But when our tail gunner got his shoes shot off of him, I mean, pretty close. And when that thing hit the back of my head and blew the plexiglass off, I mean, I don't want to get that close again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies from other planes, other crews?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No. We -- yeah, we lost the -- we didn't associate too much with other crews . Because you kind of knew the, you're here today and maybe gone tomorrow, you know. So you didn't get close to any -- you knew them, talked to them, but I mean you didn't get close to them at all, other than our own crew. We basically, we did everything while we were over there, everything we did was as a crew. Of course then, when you got leave, I mean, the whole crew got leave. It wasn't just you. So we went together, and pretty well stuck together almost all the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Get any U.S.O. shows over there?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or other shows?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No. Not a one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nothing. Bob Hope didn't show up out at the base?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No. We were at the base that Clark Gable flew a mission from.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh really?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah. It was 92nd bomb group at that time. It wasn't us. But he was at our base. Another little, there's Carl Galbes, course he's dead. He landed at our base one time. But of course I didn't know it till after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that again?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Carl Galbes. He passed away about five or six years ago. Ain't too much of us left, is there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Clark Gable wasn't flying out of there when you were there, was he?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was before?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, that was before, before I was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And this is the 8th Air Force that you were a part of; right?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yes. The first bomb, 41st bomb wing, I think it was. There was three of us. 303rd bomb group, Groton, 379 to 381st, we formed one wing. And we were all bunched in one area. But so, we were, all the triangle, we were Triangle P, 379th, a Triangle K, and then Wolsworth was Triangle C I think. But that's how they designated us. All triangles were first division, all square tail markings were the third division; second division had slashes. I did fly at the Battle of the Bulge; but that was my last mission, actually.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: We were gone just before the weather hit. We flew a mission. We couldn't get back into our base, we landed someplace in southern England. It was kind of strange. It was an English base. We couldn't raise the tower. And because I'm a different frequency, we didn't know what frequency to get on. So well, the only thing to do, we just lined up and came in one at a time. And our practice, the 8th Air Force was, when we came back, all landing, or take-off was the same thing, there was one turning off the end of the runway, the first guy to land, the second guy was about halfway down the runway, and the third guy was just touching down. So you could say there was three to a runway. Here's my lieutenant colonel. But so there was basically three planes on the runway at the same time. And what was I going to say?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About landing at the English base?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Oh, and they were horrified, seeing three planes on the runway at the same time. And of course it was Christmas, just before Christmas. And well, when we -- we all got down all right, but then we ate them out of house and home. 'Cause we were there I think the next day, yeah, we were there, well, all the next day; then the day after, we flew to, I don't know which base, but it was one of ours. We bombed up and flew that mission right after the weather broke at Bastogne. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that your final mission then?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: That was my final. Another thing. When I say I flew to Cologne, I mean, we might have -- when you flew a mission, you had more than one target. It was, you're all in the same area. For example, in Cleveland here, one might be bombing the steel works, and another one is bombing aluminum factory, but all within the same area. So when you get the thing back, which mission did you fly? You look at it, your group flew two missions that day. Which one were you on? I don't know. Nobody knew. We didn't know. We were in the general area. But probably my most scariest thing I had, other than that hit on the turret, was, if I'm not mistaken, it was Cologne. And somehow or other the, we, B-24's were, we were on our bomb run, the B-24's suddenly appeared off to, from the side. And we were too close for comfort. In fact, I think one plane did crash with one of them. Not our group. I mean, I read about it in the papers later, that there was some kind of a mix-up there. Which is not unusual, because I mean, they flew a different -- the B-24 didn't handle too well at altitude, where the B-17 was an excellent high-altitude plane. So they didn't usually fly as high as we did. They were close. But so they were below us. But I mean -- how do you explain? When you flew in a formation, there was, you were staggered. One was up here, one was down here, and one was here, as far as the few squadrons are concerned. Of course they were flying the same way. So their high guy and our low group could very well be too damn close for comfort.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: And I think that's what happened. My own observation. I have nothing --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would they try to bomb the same target?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: That I don't know. I know we intersected. In fact, I got a picture of it someplace. And I mean, that came out later. I think it was of the same --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your plane have a name?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't bother with that?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No. Well, we didn't fly the same plane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Okay.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: You know, we had no -- you flew whatever they told you go out to this hard stand, well, they didn't tell you to go. They took you there. And that's the plane you flew. But one time we, we, a radio engine -- I have pictures of it somewhere, if you know what they look like. And the pushrods that go up to the, operate the valves, they're in front of the engine. And we got hit in one of those pushrods. And it was, I didn't notice at the time, but it was just a tiny hole. But to look at the airplane, you'd say, oh my god, there was oil all over the place. And it looked -- it was just a film, you know. And of course, when the pilot was going to turn, he wanted to feather the engine. So he asked me what to do, and I told him to let it run. The one way you could tell, you didn't want to run, the same oil that the engine used for lubrication was the oil that controlled the propeller. If you run out of oil, you had no control of the propeller, and it would run away, and it would yank the engine right off the airplane, or break off and go through the airplane. You didn't know which way it was going to go, or where. So you had to feather them before you reached the point of no oil. And I suppose he was concerned. He wanted to feather it. And I says, "Hell no. We're way over Germany. I'm going to get home." So he didn't feather. He wanted to, but he never feathered. And part of it was from what I told you before, when we, the engine was running away, when we first going overseas, because at that time, when we come back, we were met by the colonel of the base, and he asked the pilot, you know, what he did. He said, "Did you ask your engineer?" He says, "Yeah." He says, "Well, let's see the records." 'Cause you know, we carry records. He says, "Next time," he says, "I advise you to listen to him." And he did. And as I said, that one time, almost to our detriment. But so he didn't feather it. And we came back. I mean, we lost, each engine carried, I think it was 20 gallons of oil. So we lost about half of it. But we got back without feathering the prop. So that was no problem. It turned out to be no problem. But the way you used to tell was, if the engine temperature, cylinder head temperature, which there was a gauge for, if that started to rise rapidly, or if your oil pressure started -- not the oil pressure, the oil temperature started to rise, you feathered immediately. So that's what we watched for, you know. When we, excuse me. So all the oil coming out, you know, it, to look at it, it looked horrible, you know. But it was really a minor, a minor incident.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the process of feathering the prop? What would you do then?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: There's a button, a red button, when you're feathered, you just hit the red button. There's one for each engine, right across the board. And when you feathered, the propellers, instead of being flat-wise, they turned, face directly into the engine; and you do it so that, when the propeller was just like a fan, will --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: -- not because you're -- if you can't feather it, and the engine is dead, the wind from the forward motion will keep it turning. Of course, it runs out of oil, and then it seizes, and that's why they break off.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just rips it right off it?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: You don't know what it can do. It can rip the wing off, it can rip the engine off, it can be nothing more than the propeller, or nothing. You don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that turns it in so that the wind doesn't -- there's no resistance?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, the blades are facing directly into the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wind goes right past it.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Instead of affecting it?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly. I've heard it a million times, and I know what it looks like, but I've never asked anybody.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah. No, one --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Than one thing I do have to say, I mean, I took my schooling on, very seriously. Which a lot of, a lot of us didn't. But I mean, I was, I don't know why I was different about it. But I was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you were thinking and feeling when you flew that last mission?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, not really. There was, we had no opposition. I don't even know if we had any anti-aircraft fire. It was just, just we were joy-riding, I mean as far as, we didn't see any German planes. We, very meager flak, if any. I don't even remember if we had any flak.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that is with a during the Bulge, Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: That was at the Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was Bastogne the mission that you flew on your last mission? Near Bastogne?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Somewhere, after the weather broke?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: It was in the area. Either we were bombing the air fields or their transportation or bridges or something in support of the ground troops, so the Germans couldn't move. Exactly what the target was, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you wouldn't be bombing Bastogne, because we were there.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: We did once.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Outside of Bastogne?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: We did once.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you accidentally hit?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: We dropped on the wrong -- after the mission, of course, I mean, you get the critique, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: And looking at the maps, and there was the shape of the forest, bombing of woods where there was German concentration of tanks, they were hiding them. And we picked the wrong forest. And we, as an afterthought, when you looked at it, the two of them were very similar. So it, it's no excuse; but I mean, we just picked the wrong, wrong bunch of trees to bomb. And as it turned out, we were, dropped them on our own troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: But that was, well, that was way before Bastogne. Again, I can't tell you where it was. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they try to lay out markers on the ground to tell you where to bomb, or smoke or anything?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Smoke, they did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: They shot up, our own antiaircraft would shoot up various color flares. And they tried to -- they're timed. They're set to explode at a certain altitude. So we didn't want them trying to hit us, but they were shooting ahead of us so that we could see them. You don't drop before you pass the, those things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Those things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Of course we had the -- I was not involved with the ground, the spotters, on the ground, talking through the, to the pilot or bombardier.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your plane wasn't communicating with them?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were communicating with the --

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah. I was not involved.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: But somebody in our airplane was communicating with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Talking to them.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Probably the lead plane, whoever it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Was communicating with them, and telling them. Because they could look up and say, well, you're directly overhead, but we didn't know that, you know. When they passed the front lines, why then they had liaison guys that tell you, okay, now you're safe. But then even then, I mean, you wanted to bomb close as you could to their troops, you know, without hitting them. If, we considered it a direct hit if we landed within a thousand yards of our aiming point. That's quite a --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: -- pretty big circle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's more than a half mile; right?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: They don't fall straight down. They wobble. And if you were a little bit this way, they'll just get out, whatever. So you didn't, we considered it a direct hit if we were within a thousand. I said thousand yards. I think I meant thousand feet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Thousand feet.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: So we consider that -- of course a lot of times we didn't, never even saw the ground, with the radar. Those were the scariest moments, because climbing through the cloud, the clouds, 'cause, well, when you got 500, 700 planes in the air, there's a lot of, a lot of things you can hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: And they did on occasion. Never happened to us, that I can recall. But I mean, to our group. But it did happen. And well, landings were always a little bit critical, if you were hit. And you actually, if you had a flat tire, you, sometimes you knew it and sometimes you didn't, you know. So when you landed, your end did one of these.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any rough landings like that?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Only one, when the landing gear didn't want to cooperate. One wheel went down, but the other one didn't. So had to crank it down, and pray.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Or fortunately it stayed up. But we came in with feathered engines a couple of times. But we didn't have to feather them over Germany. They were feathered long after we had been to the target.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how many engines did you lose? Were you able to bring it back with two engines?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: You could. I mean, you were alone if you did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: You couldn't keep up with them. But yeah, you could come back. In fact, there was a couple instances they kept them going on one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm glad you said that; because I've heard that before, and somebody disputed that with me; said that that wasn't -- I said no, I've heard it before, that you can fly on one. Not far and fast.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, not far. I mean, if you were on one, you were not going to make it home. No doubt about it. But you could fly so that you weren't going to make a emergency crash landing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Crash landing, emergency, I mean beyond the normal --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Some control anyway.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, a little bit of control.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: And there are a lot of funny -- they had some of them, where the guy, the plane bombed out, or the guys jumped, I mean, because of a hit, and nobody in the airplane, the god damn thing just keeps on flying, won't go down 'til it runs out of gas. And sometimes they went down when you didn't want them to.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: But that was life with us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned that one letter that you wrote back home. Do you have any other memories of mail call?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well, no. I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't get a lot of mail from home, or --

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Oh yeah. We always got it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Packages, whatever?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, we always got -- you have to understand, we led a relatively easy life. When we weren't in combat, I mean, you know, actually flying, I mean there was not, nothing too much out of the norm. We had a bed to sleep in, there was, chow was always going to be there. So our life, other than the time we were flying, was pretty good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I don't know if maybe, probably others told you, but in the 8th Air Force, the flying personnel, whether you were officer or not, you had officer's rations. The ground crew did not. And one more incident, I was not involved, mention chow hall, we were lined up to go eat, just as the mission was returning, and one plane crashed, oh, about here to the house, away from us. He didn't make the runway. And of course, they exploded and burned. And you don't want to see that. I mean, as I recall, nobody, you know, the sudden hush, you know, lined up, everybody's talking, and all of a sudden there's just, somebody threw a switch, and complete quiet. We watched them go into the trees. They burned, and I don't think anybody ate supper that night. I know I didn't. But, oh, one more thing, kind of derogatory, but our copilot was not very skilled. He, he come in for a landing, he would, I don't know how -- he was extremely, I mean, there's practically -- his arms were locked, you know. And so we have to shoot landings with him, and we dreaded it. Because as I say, he wasn't too skilled, and he'd -- the guys, the checkered wagon at the end of the runway, when they knew he was shooting landings, there was nobody in that checkered runway. Because he did some things there, one time he, to correct the airplane on the runway on take-off, 'cause you know, you don't go straight down the runway. You control it with the rudder. And he controlled it with the brakes. Or he tried to. And you don't, I don't want to go do that again, either. So I mean, in the air, he was a decent pilot. But take-offs and landings, he was not very good at at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is there a reason why he would be doing the landings instead of the pilot?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, yes, it, he was a pilot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: He had to be, to do landings. Copilot or not, he has to do them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Has to do them.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: 'Cause you know, he made pilot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: When, he was flying his own crew when he crashed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would he be doing that maybe half the time or whatever, or --

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No. You had --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Once in a while?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: I don't know what the exact regulations are; but they had to make, to maintain proficiency, they had to do a certain number of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Take-off and landings?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Take-off and landings, and the whole bit. He was, part of the routine, you didn't do it at missions or anything, you know. But in between missions or whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When he went down, he was not doing a take-off and landing, was he?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: He was landing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was landing?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: The, the story that we got was that he was making -- they had three runways on the east coast of England. They were strictly emergency. Not strictly emergency, but I mean basically, the runways were huge. You could land a 17 on one end of it, let it roll to a stop without brakes, and still have room to take off. That's how big they were. And that's where he was landing. But he did not land down the runway. He landed at an angle to the runway. And he crashed into a Mosquito, and another plane. But I mean, you're not there. Nobody knows the circumstances that led up to it. But I guess that's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And when you think about World War II, do any other vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Oh, none. You mean directly to the war, or personal?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Personal, sure.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: No, except I was A.W.O.L. a couple times. Didn't get caught.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How'd that happen?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Well this is after the war. I was at Chanute Airfield in Illinois, going to Langley Field. That was after the, that was in Chanute to start training for B-29's, at, why I was there. But then they cancelled all that. And we were transferred to Langley Field, Virginia; and of course, going through Cincinnati, and it just so happened I was the ranking non-com at the time. And there was 12 of us, or something around there. So when we got to Cincinnati, I told the guys, I said, "I don't know about you, but I'm pretty close to home. I'm going home." So we all got together, and we decided we would meet at, in Washington D.C., and go in as a group. So on the way home, there was a private sitting next to me on the train; and the M.P. comes down, he asks him for his leave papers, and he doesn't say a word to me. So the guy says, "Hey, you don't ask him." He told him, "Mind your own business." And here I'm the one that's A.W.O.L. But then I came home, and my mother was all excited, she said, "What are you doing home?" You know, I -- "Close, came home." She says, "But you're A.W.O.L." "Yeah," I say. "Well, I'm going to call them and tell you where you are." "Oh no you're not." So she didn't. But as luck would have it, I was the last one in Washington. But we did, we get there, had to report to whoever he was, and he looks up at me, and he says, "You're a little bit late, ain't you?" Was the sum total of it. Well, there's another incident, too. When I was at Langley, there was a hurricane coming in. So they were flying all the planes out. And we came into -- we were, our destination was Wright Field in Dayton here. And it was at night. And we were in contact with the tower, the pilot is. And he's cleared to land. Well, he's coming in for landing, says geez, damn runway looks awful short. We're over Richmond, Indiana. So we woke up a lot of people that night. The engines went from idling to full power. And when you're down that low, you rattled a few windows. But it was funny. I mean, well as the engineer of course, my station was right behind the, right between the two pilots, standing up. I mean, there was no seat. You're standing up, my job of course was to watch the instruments, and you know, stuff like that. You can see whatever the pilot sees, you know. You're looking out the same window. And it did look kind of small. But we were there, I guess three or four days. The hurricane blew over, we went back. But I couldn't get out of the Army. Because I was at Langley Field, discharge center. Well, I wasn't assigned there. I was only on temporary duty there, so I couldn't get discharged. I'm at Dayton Field, same thing. I got way more than enough points to get discharged. Can't get out. So they ship me back to Langley. Same story. Finally they shipped us all to Waco, Texas; and I got discharged from Waco, Texas. I'm only, at most, four, five hours from home, I can't get -- I gotta go someplace where I'm, and they had to pay a per diem, they had to pay you by the mile, you know, coming home. So that cost them a lot of money to send me home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That way, yeah. Geez. So when did you come back to the States after your tour of duty, in early '45?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You have a little reunion with your family when you first got back?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Oh sure. Actually, I don't think it was unique with everybody; but after I came back, from the time we landed at Camp Kilmer, I flew back, I volunteered for K.P. to come back home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh really?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: On a hospital ship. My duty was to serve dinners to, or meals to three patients, you know. And that was, I became the fourth patient, because it was the English ship, you ever try eating fish for breakfast? All of a sudden I was carrying four trays instead of three. But another odd thing, too. Walking around the ship, looking at this girl, she's awful familiar. She is my neighbor. She was in the Red Cross. And next house down from me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Out in the middle of the Atlantic, and you meet somebody, your neighbor. That was strictly coincidence, you know. That was another thing I kind of -- the Red Cross, on base, they were very good. We had a Red Cross segment on base. But if you went to town or something, I mean, nothing was free. You paid for everything you got. And it kind of ground my gears. The Salvation Army was just the opposite: You paid for nothing. Wasn't that we couldn't afford it. It was just the idea of it, you know. As I said, we made more money, I made more money than the English did working. So, and I mean, of course I was paying no taxes or nothing on it, where they were. So I mean -- and you have to admire them. I mean, they got along on very little. If that happened in the United States, I mean, we'd be bitching forever, you know. But I mean, they just, I guess they knew it was inevitable, and they were resigned to it; and I never heard anybody complain about, you know, rationing, or foods or nothing. And the thing is, and their standard of living was, it was in a few homes; and what we consider, we would not even consider, they consider it pretty much standard, you know. And we would be throwing the furniture and the stuff out long before that. Of course, it was the war time there, too. I mean, that always changes things, too. You put up with a lot more than you otherwise would. But as I said before, I mean, the English people were nice to me. I had no complaints whatsoever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Pretty close.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pretty close?

sp.speaker: Frank Girman
sp.p: Yeah, I can't think of anything else.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, you've answered all the questions.
